hints: Focus on what adding NaQ actually adds to the equilibrium mixture, since it fully dissociates in water.

Notice that $\text{Q}^-$ is already a product in $\text{HQ(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+\text{(aq)} + \text{Q}^-\text{(aq)}$, so think about how Le Chatelier's principle responds to extra product.
Connect a fall in $[\text{H}^+]$ to pH using $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$, remembering they always move in opposite directions.
walkthrough:
**Identify what is added**

Think of NaQ as a source of extra $\text{Q}^-$ ions. It is a soluble salt, so it dissociates completely:
$$\text{NaQ(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+\text{(aq)} + \text{Q}^-\text{(aq)}$$

**Apply Le Chatelier to the weak acid equilibrium**

The weak acid equilibrium is:
$$\text{HQ(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+\text{(aq)} + \text{Q}^-\text{(aq)}$$
Adding $\text{Q}^-$ increases the concentration of a product, so the position of equilibrium shifts to the left to use it up.

**Link to $[\text{H}^+]$ and pH**

Shifting left removes $\text{H}^+$, so $[\text{H}^+\text{(aq)}]$ decreases. Since pH is the opposite measure of acidity:
$$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]$$
A lower $[\text{H}^+]$ means a higher pH. This is the common ion effect and the basis of a buffer solution.

options.A: Half right, half wrong. $[\text{H}^+]$ does decrease, but pH cannot also decrease. pH and $[\text{H}^+]$ always change in opposite directions, so this pair is impossible.
options.B: Correct and reassuring. Extra $\text{Q}^-$ shifts the equilibrium $\text{HQ} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{Q}^-$ to the left, suppressing dissociation. $[\text{H}^+]$ falls and pH therefore rises.
options.C: Incorrect, this is the opposite shift. It assumes added $\text{Q}^-$ drives dissociation forward. In fact Le Chatelier predicts a shift backward to remove the added common ion, so $[\text{H}^+]$ falls, not rises.
options.D: Incorrect and also an impossible pair. $[\text{H}^+]$ cannot increase here, and $[\text{H}^+]$ and pH cannot both increase together. This choice ignores the common ion effect.
